• Recommendations for energy-saving measures, such as improvements to insulation, windows, ventilation controls or installation of more efficient heating systems.

Here are the main advantages of installing photovoltaic (PV) solar panels on a building:

1. Reduced energy costs  
   • By generating electricity on‐site you substantially lower your monthly utility bills.  
   • Self-consumption of solar power shields you against rising retail electricity prices.  
   • Any surplus power can often be sold back to the grid (depending on local net‐metering or feed-in tariffs).

2. Improved energy performance and property value  
   • Adding solar panels typically improves a building’s Energy Performance Certificate (EPC) rating or “energiklass.”  
   • A higher EPC rating can translate into higher market value and make the property more attractive to buyers or tenants.  
   • Solar installations signal a commitment to sustainability, which is increasingly valued in both commercial and residential real estate markets.

3. Environmental benefits  
   • Solar PV generates electricity without burning fossil fuels, cutting your building’s carbon footprint.

• Emergency lighting (in case of power failure)  
  – Minimum of 1 lux along the centerline of the escape route (including stair flights)

In most Swedish multi-family or public buildings the stairwell (trapphus) is treated as a secondary or commun­al space rather than a fully heated living area. The general recommendation is:

• Maintain a minimum operative temperature of around 12 °C to avoid frost, condensation and cold-air stratification.  
• For winter comfort and to prevent excessive heat loss, many designers and building owners choose 14–16 °C as a compromise between energy efficiency and user comfort.  

Key points:  
• Below about 12 °C you risk cold surfaces, ice formation on metal handrails and discomfort when moving between floors.  
• Above 16–18 °C yields diminishing comfort gains and drives up heating costs unnecessarily in a space that is only used intermittently.  
• If the stairwell shares ventilation with corridors or entry lobbies, co-ordinate set-points so airflow balances and you don’t over-heat one zone to warm another.

Ventilation balancing refers to the process of adjusting and fine-tuning the airflows in a building’s mechanical ventilation system so that the volume of supplied air matches the volume of exhausted air in each zone or room. Proper balancing has a direct impact on overall energy use in several ways:

1. Reduced Heat Loss and Gain  
   • In an unbalanced system, you may be supplying more air (and therefore more cold or hot outside air) than you are exhausting—or vice versa.  
   • Oversupply of cold outdoor air in winter (or hot outdoor air in summer) forces the heating or cooling plant to work harder to maintain setpoint temperatures, increasing energy consumption.  
   • A balanced system minimizes unnecessary conditioning of outdoor air, so less energy is spent on heating in winter and on cooling/dehumidifying in summer.
